title: Joseph's Stewardship
overview: Genesis 47 details the critical phase of Israel's family settling in Egypt during a severe famine. Joseph, now a powerful leader under Pharaoh, brings his father Jacob and his brothers into the land of Goshen, securing them the best territory to dwell and prosper. The chapter reveals Joseph's wise management of Egypt's resources during famine, including the acquisition of land and livestock for Pharaoh, and the establishment of a system where Egyptians become servants to Pharaoh in exchange for sustenance. It also highlights Jacob's final years in Egypt and his request for burial in Canaan, emphasizing faith in God's promises. This chapter is pivotal as it sets the stage for Israel's growth in Egypt and the eventual Exodus.
structure:
**Verses 1-11: Arrival and Settlement in Goshen.** Joseph informs Pharaoh of his family’s arrival, and Pharaoh grants them the land of Goshen, the best in Egypt, for their dwelling. Joseph introduces his family to Pharaoh, and Jacob blesses Pharaoh, symbolizing respect and divine favor.

**Verses 12-26: Management of the Famine and Economic Policies.** Joseph feeds his family and the Egyptians during the famine, first by selling grain for money, then for livestock, and finally by purchasing all the land for Pharaoh. He institutes a system where Egyptians give a fifth of their produce to Pharaoh, establishing a lasting law except for the priests’ land.

**Verses 27-31: Jacob’s Later Years and Deathbed Request.** Israel dwells in Goshen, prospers, and lives seventeen years in Egypt. As his death approaches, Jacob requests Joseph to promise to bury him in Canaan, affirming the family’s connection to the promised land.

keyVerses.text: The land of Egypt is before thee; in the best of the land make thy father and brethren to dwell; in the land of Goshen let them dwell: and if thou knowest any men of activity among them, then make them rulers over my cattle.
keyVerses.significance: This verse highlights Pharaoh’s favor toward Joseph’s family, granting them prime land and authority. It underscores God’s providence in preserving Israel and positioning them for future blessing.

keyVerses.text: And Joseph bought all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh; for the Egyptians sold every man his field, because the famine prevailed over them: so the land became Pharaoh's.
keyVerses.significance: Joseph’s acquisition of all Egyptian land for Pharaoh demonstrates his administrative wisdom and God's sovereign provision. It sets a precedent for divine control over nations and resources.

keyVerses.text: And it shall come to pass in the increase, that ye shall give the fifth part unto Pharaoh, and four parts shall be your own, for seed of the field, and for your food, and for them of your households, and for food for your little ones.
keyVerses.significance: This verse establishes a system of taxation and stewardship during famine recovery, reflecting order and justice. It also foreshadows later biblical principles of tithing and provision.

keyVerses.text: And Israel dwelt in the land of Egypt, in the country of Goshen; and they had possessions therein, and grew, and multiplied exceedingly.
keyVerses.significance: This verse marks the beginning of Israel’s growth in Egypt, fulfilling God’s promise to multiply Abraham’s descendants. It is foundational for understanding Israel’s future as a nation.

keyVerses.text: But I will lie with my fathers, and thou shalt carry me out of Egypt, and bury me in their buryingplace. And he said, I will do as thou hast said.
keyVerses.significance: Jacob’s burial request emphasizes faith in God’s covenant promises regarding the land of Canaan. It expresses hope beyond Egypt and loyalty to God’s chosen inheritance.

characters.name: Joseph
characters.description: Son of Jacob, elevated to a high position in Egypt. In this chapter, he manages the famine crisis, secures land and provisions for his family and Egypt, and acts as a faithful steward of Pharaoh’s resources.

characters.name: Jacob (Israel)
characters.description: Patriarch of Israel and father of Joseph. He relocates to Egypt, blesses Pharaoh, and makes a solemn request to be buried in Canaan, affirming the family’s covenantal identity.

characters.name: Pharaoh
characters.description: The Egyptian ruler who welcomes Joseph’s family into Goshen and entrusts Joseph with authority. His decisions facilitate Israel’s settlement and Egypt’s survival during famine.

themes.description: God’s sovereign hand is evident in Joseph’s rise, the provision during famine, and the preservation of Israel. This chapter shows how God works through human leadership to fulfill His promises.
Joseph exemplifies faithful stewardship of resources during crisis, managing Egypt’s economy wisely. This reflects the biblical principle of using God-given gifts responsibly.
Jacob’s burial request and the family’s settlement in Goshen underscore their ongoing connection to God’s covenant promises about the land of Canaan.
The chapter highlights God’s provision through Joseph’s administration, showing that God sustains His people even in times of severe scarcity.

historicalContext: Genesis 47 is set during a severe famine in the ancient Near East, likely in the second millennium BC, when Egypt was a dominant regional power. The land of Goshen, located in the northeastern Nile Delta, was fertile and suitable for shepherding, making it ideal for Joseph’s family, who were shepherds by trade. Egyptian society was highly stratified, with Pharaoh as the supreme ruler. The economic system allowed for land ownership but also centralized authority, which Joseph leveraged to manage famine relief. The practice of exchanging livestock and land for food reflects ancient Near Eastern customs of survival during famine and the consolidation of land under royal control.

theologicalInterpretations.description: This perspective emphasizes God’s sovereign providence in orchestrating Joseph’s rise and the preservation of Israel. Joseph’s stewardship is seen as a God-ordained means to fulfill covenant promises, highlighting divine sovereignty over history.

Dispensationalists view this chapter as a key moment in God’s unfolding plan for Israel, marking their physical relocation to Egypt as a distinct dispensation before the Exodus. Joseph’s role is seen as a type of Christ, providing salvation during crisis.

Early church interpreters often saw Joseph as a Christ-figure, with his provision during famine prefiguring Christ’s spiritual provision. Jacob’s burial request is interpreted as a testimony to the hope of resurrection and the promised land.

crossReferences.connection: Affirms that God works all things together for good, as seen in Joseph’s management of famine for Israel’s preservation.
Recalls Joseph’s story and God’s providence in Egypt, paralleling the events of Genesis 47.
Describes Israel’s multiplication in Egypt, fulfilling the promise noted in Genesis 47:27.
Commends Joseph for his faith in God’s promises, including his instructions about his bones, connecting to Jacob’s burial request.
Highlights the wisdom of diligent planning and stewardship, exemplified by Joseph’s management during famine.

application: Trust God’s providence even in difficult circumstances, knowing He works through human leaders and events for His purposes.
Practice faithful stewardship of resources, managing what God has given wisely and responsibly.
Honor God’s promises by living with hope and faithfulness, as Jacob did in requesting burial in the promised land.
Respond to crises with wise planning and generosity, reflecting Joseph’s example in providing for many during famine.
Recognize God’s sovereignty over nations and circumstances, submitting to His authority in all areas of life.
conclusion: Genesis 47 powerfully illustrates God’s providential care for His people through Joseph’s faithful stewardship and wise leadership. The chapter underscores the importance of trusting God’s promises, managing resources responsibly, and maintaining covenantal faith even in hardship. For believers today, it offers encouragement that God is sovereign over all circumstances and works through His servants to provide and preserve His people. The enduring lessons of faith, wisdom, and hope in God’s plan remain vital for Christian living.

outline.heading: Arrival and Introduction to Pharaoh
outline.description: Joseph informs Pharaoh of his family’s arrival and presents five brothers to Pharaoh, establishing their identity and purpose.

outline.heading: Settlement in Goshen
outline.description: Pharaoh grants Joseph’s family the best land in Goshen to dwell, and Jacob blesses Pharaoh, symbolizing mutual respect and divine favor.

outline.heading: Famine Management and Economic Transactions
outline.description: Joseph feeds his family and the Egyptians, acquires land and livestock for Pharaoh, and institutes a system of taxation to sustain the nation.

outline.heading: Israel’s Growth and Jacob’s Final Request
outline.description: Israel prospers in Egypt, and Jacob, nearing death, requests burial in Canaan, affirming faith in God’s promises and the family’s heritage.
